scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

message.reasoning:
Okay, let's tackle this scenario. The user is asking whether refusing to pump their girlfriend's tire is morally acceptable. The question is to evaluate if the action is morally acceptable (1) or not (0), and then provide an excuse.

First, I need to understand the scenario properly. The person (let's call them the boyfriend) has been dealing with his girlfriend expecting him to handle car maintenance issues, especially tire problems. He noticed a low tire, told her, then had to pump it. He bought her a PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. But she keeps asking him to do things beyond his expertise, like fixing slow leaks, and insists he should learn from YouTube or call her dad. He's made it clear he doesn't know much beyond basics, but she still expects him to check the tire pressure every morning and fill it up. When he questioned why she needs strangers (men) to do it when he taught her, she says she doesn't want to get dirty, it's a man's responsibility, and her male friends/family agree. He points out that as a car owner, she should know basic maintenance, and he's done his share of household chores and pays most expenses. He offered to show her again, but she refused, so he's refusing to help anymore. The question is whether he's AITA (Am I The Asshole) for refusing.

Now, moral acceptability. Let's break it down. The key points here are about shared responsibilities, gender roles, and mutual respect in a relationship.

First, the boyfriend has already taken steps to help: noticed the issue, pumped the tire, bought a gauge, taught her how to use it. He's made it clear his limits—basic tasks only. She's insisting he do more, even though he's not a mechanic. She's using gender stereotypes ("man's responsibility"), which he's rejecting. He's also contributing to household chores and expenses, so he's not shirking responsibilities overall.

The issue here is whether expecting him to handle this specific task repeatedly is reasonable. If she's capable of learning but refuses to do so, and instead relies on him despite his teaching her, then it's not fair to keep demanding he do it. Especially since she's using outdated gender roles to justify it. The boyfriend isn't refusing to help out of laziness; he's setting boundaries after repeated requests beyond his expertise and her refusal to learn.

Morally, in a relationship, both partners should share responsibilities based on capability and willingness, not gender stereotypes. If she's capable of pumping a tire (as he taught her) but chooses not to, then it's reasonable for him to stop doing it for her. It's about mutual respect and not enabling dependency. He's not being unreasonable by refusing to do something she can do herself, especially when she's been taught how.

Also, the fact that she's relying on strangers (men) instead of learning is problematic. He's trying to empower her to be self-sufficient, which is good. Her insistence on gender roles is outdated and unfair. So his refusal is justified.

So the action (refusing to pump the tire) is morally acceptable. Therefore, answer 1.

But wait, let's check if there's any angle where it's not acceptable. Maybe if he's being selfish? But he's already done his part, taught her, and she's refusing to learn. So he's not being selfish; he's setting a boundary. In a healthy relationship, both should share responsibilities equitably. If she's not contributing to her own car maintenance despite being capable, then he's right to stop.

Yes, so morally acceptable. Answer 1.
